A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ROBIN research, with matching authors, methods, and original benchmarks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, timing experiments, and ablations on BENDINGBEAM, IMPACTPLATE, and DEFORMINGPLATE, including rollout visualizations in Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation evaluations and adds BSMS comparisons, truncation diagnostics, an architecture ablation, and large-mesh transfer results.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 introduces configurable intermediate denoising truncation. v1 already described a first-step shortcut and separately trained shorter-diffusion models; v2 generalizes early stopping within one trained model. The AMPN architecture, diffusion objective, and underlying rolling inference remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: The three original physical tasks remain. v2 adds BENDINGBEAMLARGE and a small-to-large mesh transfer scenario, with 8,897 average nodes versus 744 for BENDINGBEAM (Appendix B, Table 1). This extends coverage to substantially larger input meshes within the existing beam-bending task.

E2.justification: The principal comparison expands from MGN and HCMT to include BSMS on all three benchmarks, including qualitative rollout comparisons. BSMS was only cited in v1. v2 also evaluates an HCMT-backbone control retaining DDPMs and ROBI, materially strengthening comparisons with alternative hierarchical architectures.

E3.justification: v2 adds a truncation sweep on one trained model, displacement-gradient evaluation, and fine-tuning versus training from scratch on large meshes. Appendix C changes RMSE normalization from 1/N_i to 1/(N_i N_j) inside the square root. Appendix D swaps reported HCMT training budgets from 2M/3M to 3M/2M iterations for IMPACTPLATE/DEFORMINGPLATE. These are reported protocol revisions; they do not establish whether existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether AMPNs outperform an HCMT backbone under the same diffusion framework, how truncation affects displacement gradients and accumulated mesh damage, and whether pretraining aids larger-mesh learning. These appear in Figures 6–8 and 14–15. The K=5 and K=10 experiments already existed in v1 and are reorganized as ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting in Appendix C; v1 already displays error bars and individual runs. v2 restates and extends this practice to added results, without introducing additional repetitions, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds BSMS, HCMT-backbone, truncation, gradient-error, and transfer results. Table 3 reports large-mesh RMSE of 77.59 versus 215.50, in units of 10^-3, for fine-tuned versus from-scratch models. The reported BENDINGBEAM default-versus-one-step timing overhead changes from approximately 71% to 58%. Revised protocols limit direct cross-version performance comparisons, and some Table 3 entries disagree with plots, notably BENDINGBEAM MGN values and uncertainty in Figure 4.

T1.justification: Appendix C revises the explicit mathematical definition of RMSE by adding normalization over feature count. The principal DDPM and message-passing equations remain essentially unchanged, and neither version provides new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The core claims about diffusion refinement, hierarchical message passing, accuracy, and accelerated inference remain. v2's introduction additionally claims efficient transfer to much larger meshes while maintaining near-FEM accuracy, extending the claimed applicability beyond the original evaluations.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretation of truncation-induced mesh degradation and the IMPACTPLATE tradeoff between lower displacement error and higher gradient error, hypothesizing low-frequency stabilization versus high-frequency refinement. This qualifies the accuracy–speed interpretation beyond v1's global-error analysis. The SO(3) limitation also changes from restricted applicability to tensor fields and anisotropic materials to potential accuracy benefits for orientation-sensitive predictions.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the future code/data-release promise with reported availability and a project link. It adds BSMS implementation access and detailed training settings, mesh-size statistics, expanded compute accounting, and clearer AMG implementation instructions. Table 1 removes the simulator-name column. These are documentation and access-information changes; external availability was not verified.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 66 works. Related work adds an explicit explanation of physics-informed MeshGraphNets as a complementary FEM-based training approach, while BSMS becomes an evaluated comparator. The overall positioning relative to hierarchical GNNs and diffusion simulators remains stable.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendices A–E remain. v2 clarifies the rolling prediction/state-update explanation, streamlines coarsening prose, corrects terminology, and reorganizes variants and results into clearer subsections. A NeurIPS checklist is added, but most existing narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds gradient-error, truncation, and large-mesh figures plus a comprehensive numerical Table 3. Existing benchmark and rollout displays gain BSMS, the ablation display expands, and inference plots change their displayed variants and legends. The coarsening illustration moves from main-text Figure 3 to appendix Figure 10; Table 1 changes columns and adds the large-mesh row.

improvement.justification: The HCMT-backbone control and gradient/truncation diagnostics address important gaps in v1: attributing gains to the architecture and detecting local failures hidden by displacement RMSE. Larger-mesh transfer evidence further strengthens applicability. Unexplained protocol revisions and discrepancies between some plots and Table 3 limit numerical reliability, but the added controls and failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.
